title: Science Lab
subtitle: A lab book with maths and graphs, and four benches to pour, mix, heat and measure at
description: A lab book with typeset formulas, sliders that work out density, graphs to drag and a checked answer; and four close-up benches: make vinegar and baking soda fizz, titrate an acid with an indicator, layer liquids by density, and dissolve salt and boil it dry.

actions.text: Welcome to the science lab. Read the lab book in the middle, then walk up to a bench and click it.

actions.content:
Lab book

Welcome to the lab. This book has what you need for the four benches. Turn the pages, move the sliders, drag the points.

On a bench, tap a bottle to pick it up, then tap a container to pour into it.

Density

Density says how much stuff is packed into a space:

density = mass / volume

Density:

That is denser than water (1 g/mL): it would sink.

That is no denser than water: it would float.

Reading a graph: slope

Drag the two points. The slope of the line through them is how far it goes up for each step across.

slope = (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1)

Slope:

Curves

This curve is y = a x^2. Slide a and watch it open, flatten and turn over.

At x = 2, y is .

What fizzes?

Vinegar is a weak acid. Baking soda is a base. Together they make a salt, water and a gas that bubbles out:

CH3COOH + NaHCO3 → CH3COONa + H2O + CO2

A strong acid and a strong base cancel each other exactly:

HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O
Why does one drop change everything?

Near the point where they cancel, almost no acid is left. One more drop of base is then more than all the acid that remains, and the pH leaps from acid to base.

Your titration

The points you record at the Acids and bases bench appear here.

Where is the curve steepest? What is the pH there?

Check yourself

A block of metal has a mass of 54 g and a volume of 20 mL. What is its density? Give the unit.

actions.text: Right: 54 g ÷ 20 mL = 2.7 g/mL. That is the density of aluminium.
Not yet. Divide the mass by the volume, and give the unit: g/mL. Open the book to try again.

scenes.subtitle: What happens when vinegar meets baking soda?

reactions.name: Vinegar meets baking soda
reactions.note: It fizzes! A gas is bubbling out.

actions.text: Tap the vinegar to pick it up, then tap the beaker to pour some in. Then add a spoonful of baking soda. What do you see, and what happens to the temperature?
It fizzes: the acid in the vinegar and the baking soda make carbon dioxide, a gas. Watch the temperature: this reaction takes heat in. Press Record to plot it.
Over 100 mL of gas, from a few spoonfuls of powder. Where did it come from? The lab book has the equation.

scenes.subtitle: How much base cancels the acid?

actions.text: The flask holds 50 mL of acid with universal indicator: red means acid. Pour in base, and press Record after each pour to plot the pH. Can you stop when it turns green, at pH 7?
Green: neutral, pH 7. The base has cancelled the acid exactly. Add one more drop and see what the pH does. Your graph is in the lab book.

scenes.subtitle: Which liquid ends up on top?

actions.text: Pour oil, water and honey into the cylinder, in any order. Where does each one settle? A drop of blue dye shows which layer is the water.
Oil floats on water, whatever order you pour them in: a millilitre of oil has less mass than a millilitre of water. Honey has more, so it sinks under both.

scenes.subtitle: Where does the salt go, and can you get it back?

reactions.name: Salt is left behind
reactions.note: The water has gone, and the salt is back.

actions.text: Pour water into the beaker and add a spoonful of salt. Pick up the stirring rod and tap the beaker to stir. Then tap the burner to light it, and watch the graph.
The salt is dissolving: it is still there, spread through the water too finely to see. Light the burner to find out if you can get it back.
The water boiled away as steam at 100 °C, and the salt is back in the beaker. Look at the graph: the temperature climbed, then stayed flat while the water boiled.
